title: Augmenting agents with memory
lecture: CS329A Lecture 14 (Nov 7), guest lecturer Junchen Jiang (LMCache, UChicago)
big_idea: A model only sees its context window, and long contexts are slow and costly. You can give an agent more memory at three layers: let the agent page facts in and out (MemGPT), let the server reuse work it already did on the same text (KV-cache reuse: CacheBlend, LMCache), or compress a corpus into a small trained memory ahead of time (Cartridges).

papers.title: Cartridges: Lightweight and general-purpose long context representations via self-study
papers.authors: Eyuboglu, Ehrlich, Arora, Guha, Zinsley, Liu, Tennien, Rudra, Zou, Mirhoseini, Ré
papers.what: Train a small KV cache (a 'Cartridge') offline for each corpus and load it at question time instead of the whole corpus. Training on the raw text with next-token prediction generalized poorly, so they propose self-study: the model has synthetic conversations about chunks of the corpus (from generic seed prompts such as summarize, structure, ask a question), and the Cartridge is trained by context distillation to match the model's next-token distributions when the chunk is in context.
papers.result: Matched in-context learning quality on long-context benchmarks with 38.6x less memory and 26.4x higher throughput. Extended effective context on MTOB from 128k to 484k tokens. Distillation beat next-token training on MTOB (chrF 24.9 to 33.5). Initializing from the first p corpus tokens beat random vectors on LongHealth (55.3% vs 29.9%). Prefix-tuning kept MMLU near 54.7 while a memory-matched LoRA fell to 45.3. Cartridges can be composed at inference without retraining.
papers.takeaway: If one large corpus (a contract archive, a codebase) is queried thousands of times, paying once to train a compact memory can beat re-reading it each time. The training data must be varied synthetic Q&A, not the raw text.

papers.title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
papers.authors: Packer, Wooders, Lin, Fang, Patil, Stoica, Gonzalez
papers.what: Virtual context management modeled on an operating system's memory hierarchy. Main context = read-only system instructions, a writable working context, and a FIFO message queue headed by a recursive summary. External context = recall storage (all messages) and archival storage (vector-searched text). The model moves data with function calls; results are paginated; a memory-pressure warning fires at about 70% of the window and about half the queue is evicted at 100%.
papers.result: Deep memory retrieval in multi-session chat: GPT-4 accuracy 32.1% without MemGPT vs 92.5% with it (GPT-4 Turbo 35.3% vs 93.4%; GPT-3.5 Turbo 38.7% vs 66.9%). On nested key-value retrieval, GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo alone fell to 0% by 3 nesting levels, while MemGPT with GPT-4 was unaffected by depth. On document QA, MemGPT's accuracy stayed flat as more documents were retrieved, while fixed-context baselines were capped by the retriever.
papers.takeaway: Give the agent explicit memory tools (search, save a note) and a hard context budget, and keep every message in an append-only store. Check that the agent actually saves what it needs: the model decides what to remember.

papers.title: CacheBlend: Fast Large Language Model Serving for RAG with Cached Knowledge Fusion
papers.authors: Yao, Li, Liu, Ray, Cheng, Zhang, Du, Lu, Jiang
papers.what: Prefix caching only helps when a request starts with exactly the same text, which RAG rarely does. CacheBlend reuses each retrieved chunk's precomputed KV cache wherever it sits, and recomputes only a small share of tokens (15% per layer by default) chosen by KV deviation, the tokens whose KV values change most from cross-attention to earlier chunks. Recompute overlaps with loading caches from slower storage.
papers.result: Tested on Mistral-7B, Yi-34B and Llama-70B over 2WikiMQA, Musique, SAMSum and MultiNews. Versus full KV recompute: time to first token 2.2-3.3x lower and throughput 2.8-5x higher, with quality within 0.02 F1/Rouge-L. Recomputing 5-18% of tokens lost at most 0.002 F1/Rouge-L on Yi-34B. Full KV reuse without recompute was about as fast but lost 0.1-0.2 F1 on QA.
papers.takeaway: For RAG on your own GPUs, the prefill of retrieved chunks is the main latency cost. Cache chunk KV and use a serving stack that can blend it (LMCache with vLLM). Even without that, put stable text first so plain prefix caching hits.

papers.title: LMCache: An Efficient KV Cache Layer for Enterprise-Scale LLM Inference (background reading, our pick)
papers.authors: Cheng, Liu, et al. (with Junchen Jiang)
papers.what: The open-source KV cache layer from the guest lecturer's group. It moves KV caches out of GPU memory into CPU, disk or network storage and shares them across vLLM/SGLang engines and queries, supporting both prefix reuse across queries and prefill-decode disaggregation. Not an assigned course paper; added because the guest lecture is about it.
papers.result: The authors report up to 15x higher throughput when combined with vLLM on workloads such as multi-round QA and document analysis, and observe that context truncation, common in industry, can cut prefix cache hit ratio by half.
papers.takeaway: If you self-host models for repeated document work, a KV cache layer is often the cheapest speed-up available, before buying more GPUs.

terms: The text a model can see in one call. Everything else is invisible to it.
MemGPT's split: what is in the prompt now vs what is stored outside and must be fetched with a function call.
A small, writable block of notes inside the prompt that survives when old messages are evicted.
A searchable store of documents outside the window; the agent pages results in.
The key and value vectors a transformer computes for every prompt token at every layer. Reusing them skips re-reading that text.
The step where the model reads the whole prompt before writing; its time grows with prompt length.
How long a user waits before the first word appears; dominated by prefill on long prompts.
Reusing the KV cache when a new prompt starts with exactly the same text as an earlier one.
How much a token's cached KV differs from what full recompute would give; CacheBlend recomputes the tokens with the largest deviation.
A small trained KV cache that stands in for a whole corpus at question time.
Training data for a Cartridge: the model's own synthetic conversations about chunks of the corpus.
Training the model-with-Cartridge to match the next-token probabilities of the model-with-full-text.
traps: Putting a timestamp, request ID or user name at the top of the prompt. It changes the first tokens, so prefix caching never hits.
Trusting the agent to save notes. In MemGPT-style paging the model decides what to remember; if it skips a note, the fact is gone from view. Log everything and test recall.
Training a compact memory on the raw text with next-token prediction. Cartridges found it memorizes but does not generalize; the varied synthetic conversations are what make it work.
Measuring TTFT with the first call after loading the model. Load time swamps everything; warm up first.
Assuming two requests share a cache. Servers with several slots or replicas may route them apart; LMCache exists partly to share caches across engines.
check: Why does changing the first word of a long prompt make it slow again?
Prefix caching only reuses KV for an exact matching prefix; a change at the start invalidates everything after it, so the whole prompt is prefilled again.
In MemGPT, what survives when old messages are evicted from the FIFO queue?
The working context notes, a recursive summary, and the full messages in recall storage (retrievable by search).
What does CacheBlend recompute, and why not nothing?
A small share of tokens (15% per layer by default) with the highest KV deviation; reusing caches with no recompute ignores cross-attention between chunks and loses quality.
With self-study: the model generates synthetic conversations about corpus chunks, and a small KV cache is trained by context distillation to match the model's outputs when the chunk is in context.
Our notebook's 'cartridge' is text notes. What is the real one?
A set of trainable key and value vectors (a prefix-tuning style KV cache), trained with gradients while the model weights stay frozen.
